source_text: Ὁ δὲ κύριος ἀποκρίνεται διότι »τὸ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀδύνατον δυνατὸν θεῷ«. πάλιν καὶ τοῦτο μεγάλης σοφίας μεστόν ἐστιν. ὅτι καθ᾿ αὑτὸν μὲν ἀσκῶν και διαπονούμενος ἀπάθειαν ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὐδὲν ἀνύει, ἐὰν δὲ γένηται δῆλος ὑπερεπιθυμῶν τούτου καὶ διεσπουδακώς. τῇ προσθήκῃ τῆς παρὰ θεοῦ δυνάμεως περιγίνεται· βουλομέναις μὲν γὰρ ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὁ θεὸς συνεπιπνεῖ, εἰ δὲ ἀποσταῖεν τῆς προθυμίας. καὶ τὸ δοθὲν ἐκ θεοῦ πνεῦμα συνεστάλη· τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἄκοντας σῴζειν ἐστὶ βιαζομένου, τὸ δὲ αἱρουμένους χαριζομένου. οὐδὲ τῶν καθευδόντων καὶ βλακευόντων ἐστὶν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ οἱ »βιασταὶ ἁρπάζουσιν αὐτήν«· αὕτη γὰρ μόνη βία καλή, θεὸν βιάσασθαι καὶ παρὰ θεοῦ ζωὴν ἁρπάσαι, ὁ δὲ γνοὺς τοὺς βιαίως, μᾶλλον δὲ βεβαίως ἀντεχομένους [συνεχώρησεν] εἶξεν· χαίρει γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τὰ τοιαῦτα ἡττώμενος. τοιγάρτοι τούτων ἀκούσας ὁ μακάριος Πέτρος. ὁ ἐκλεκτός. ὁ ἐξαίρετος, ὁ πρῶτος τῶν μαθητῶν. ὑπὲρ οὗ μόνου καὶ ἑαυτοῦ τὸν. φόρον ὁ σωτὴρ ἐκτελεῖ, ταχέως ἥρπασε καὶ συνέβαλε τὸν λόγον. καὶ τί φησιν; »ἴδε ἡμεῖς ἀφήκαμεν πάντα καὶ ἠκολουθήσαμέν σοι.« τὰ δὲ »πάντα« εἰ μὲν τὰ κτήματα τὰ ἑαυτοῦ λέγει. τέσσαρας ὀβολοὺς ἴσως. τὸ τοῦ λόγου, καταλιπὼν μεγαλύνεται καὶ τούτων ἀνταξίαν ἀποφαίνων ἂν λάθοι τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν· εἰ δέ, ἅπερ ἄρτι νῦν λέγομεν, τὰ παλαιὰ νοητὰ κτήματα καὶ ψυχικὰ νοσήματα ἀπορρίψαντες ἕπονται κατ᾿ ἴχνος τοῦ διδασκάλου, τοῦτ᾿ ἂν ἀνάπτοιτο ἤδη τοῖς ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἐγγραφησομένοις. τοῦτο γὰρ ἀκολουθεῖν ὄντως τῷ σωτῆρι. ἀναμαρτησίαν καὶ τελειότητα τὴν ἐκείνου μετερχόμενον καὶ πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ὥσπερ κάτοπτρον κοσμοῦντα καὶ ῥυθμίζοντα τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ πάντα διὰ πάντων ὁμοίως διατιθέντα.
thought_title: God's power completes human effort; Peter's claim to have left all
orientation: Clement is explaining Jesus' answer to the disciples' astonishment, showing that salvation requires both human desire and God's enabling power, and then turns to Peter's claim that the disciples have left everything.
pass_a_gloss: But the Lord answers that 'what is impossible among humans is possible for God.' Again this too is full of great wisdom. Because by himself, practicing and laboring at freedom from passions, the human being accomplishes nothing, but if he becomes clearly desiring this exceedingly and having been zealous, by the addition of the power from God he prevails. For to souls that are willing God breathes together with them, but if they should withdraw from their eagerness, also the spirit given from God is withdrawn. For to save unwilling people is the act of one who forces, but to grant to those who choose is the act of one who gives freely. Nor is the kingdom of God of those who sleep and are sluggish, but 'the violent seize it.' For this alone is a good violence, to force God and to seize life from God. And he who knew those who violently, or rather firmly, hold fast yielded. For God rejoices being defeated in such things. Therefore, having heard these things, the blessed Peter, the chosen, the exceptional, the first of the disciples, for whom alone and for himself the Savior pays the tax, quickly seized and put together the word. And what does he say? 'Behold, we have left all things and have followed you.' But if by 'all things' he means his own possessions, having left four obols perhaps, as the saying goes, he boasts and, declaring the kingdom of heaven to be worth as much as these, he would escape notice. But if, as we were just now saying, having thrown away the old mental possessions and psychic diseases, they follow in the footsteps of the teacher, this would already be kindled for those who are to be enrolled in heaven. For this is truly to follow the Savior: pursuing sinlessness and that perfection of his, and adorning and ordering the soul toward him as toward a mirror, and disposing all things through all things in like manner.

pass_b_english: And the Lord answers: “What is impossible among humans is possible for God” (Mark 10:27). This too is full of great wisdom. For a person who practices and labors at freedom from passions on his own accomplishes nothing; but if he becomes clearly one who desires this exceedingly and has set his whole heart on it, he prevails through the addition of power from God. For God breathes together with willing souls—but if they abandon their eagerness, the Spirit given by God is also withdrawn. To save the unwilling is the act of one using force; to give grace to those who choose it is the act of one who gives freely. Nor does the kingdom of God belong to those who sleep and are idle, but “the violent seize it” (Matthew 11:12). For this alone is a noble violence: to force God, and to seize life from God. And God, knowing those who cling violently—or rather, steadfastly—yields to them. For God rejoices to be defeated in such contests.

When blessed Peter heard these things—Peter the chosen, the exceptional, the first of the disciples, for whom alone and for himself the Savior pays the tax—he quickly seized and grasped the meaning. And what does he say? “Look, we have left everything and followed you” (Mark 10:28). Now if by “everything” he means his own possessions, leaving perhaps four obols, so to speak, he exalts himself and, by valuing the kingdom of heaven at the level of these, would forget the kingdom of heaven. But if—as we have just now been saying—they have thrown away the old mental possessions and psychic diseases and follow in the footsteps of the teacher, this would already belong to those who are about to be enrolled in heaven. For this is truly to follow the Savior: to pursue his sinlessness and perfection, and to adorn and order one's soul as a mirror toward him, and to dispose all things alike in all respects.

problems.quote: To save the unwilling is the act of one who uses force; to give freely to those who choose is the act of one who gives grace.
problems.source_quote: τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἄκοντας σῴζειν ἐστὶ βιαζομένου, τὸ δὲ αἱρουμένους χαριζομένου.
problems.why: Greek says the unwilling are saved by force and the willing receive grace; English reverses agency, implying a person uses force to save.
problems.fix: The unwilling are saved by force, and the willing are given grace.

problems.quote: And he who knows those who cling to him violently—or rather, steadfastly—yields
problems.source_quote: ὁ δὲ γνοὺς τοὺς βιαίως, μᾶλλον δὲ βεβαίως ἀντεχομένους [συνεχώρησεν] εἶξεν
problems.why: ὁ δὲ refers to God (subject of previous clause), not 'he who knows'; God yields/concedes, not 'he who knows' yields.
problems.fix: And God, knowing those who cling violently—or rather steadfastly—yields
problems.ruling: Greek has God responding (ἀντεχομένους), not ‘yields’; subject is God, not ‘he who knows’.

problems.quote: he left perhaps four obols, and then boasts of this and, by declaring the kingdom of heaven to be worth that much, would unknowingly insult it
problems.source_quote: τέσσαρας ὀβολοὺς ἴσως. τὸ τοῦ λόγου, καταλιπὼν μεγαλύνεται καὶ τούτων ἀνταξίαν ἀποφαίνων ἂν λάθοι τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν
problems.why: τὸ τοῦ λόγου = 'so to speak'; 'boasts' is μεγαλύνεται (magnifies himself/glories); 'declaring...to be worth that much' is off—he makes heaven worth only that much.
problems.fix: leaving perhaps four obols, so to speak, he exalts himself and by showing the kingdom of heaven to be worth no more than these would unwittingly insult it
problems.ruling: Greek says he may lose the kingdom, not ‘insult’ it; μεγαλύνεται = boasts, not ‘declare worth’.

problems.quote: and to dispose all things in every way to be like him
problems.source_quote: καὶ πάντα διὰ πάντων ὁμοίως διατιθέμενον
problems.why: διὰ πάντων = 'through all things' or 'in all respects', not 'in every way'; ὁμοίως = 'likewise/similarly', not 'to be like him'—the phrase means making all things alike/consistent through all things.
problems.fix: and disposing all things alike in all respects
problems.ruling: Greek says arranging all things similarly, not ‘to be like him’; adds target not in source.

fixed: Agency reversed: Greek says the unwilling are saved by force and the willing are given grace; English had reversed the agents.

Mistranslation: 'so to speak' omitted; 'boasts' should be 'exalts himself'; 'declaring...worth that much' misstates the Greek, which says he makes heaven worth no more than these.
Mistranslation: διὰ πάντων means 'in all respects', not 'in every way'; ὁμοίως means 'alike', not 'to be like him'.

problems.quote: he exalts himself and by showing the kingdom of heaven to be worth no more than these would unwittingly insult it.
problems.source_quote: τὰ δὲ »πάντα« εἰ μὲν τὰ κτήματα τὰ ἑαυτοῦ λέγει. τέσσαρας ὀβολοὺς ἴσως.
problems.why: English adds commentary about exalting and insulting the kingdom not present in the Greek.
problems.fix: If “everything” means his own possessions, perhaps four obols, the statement would be limited to that meaning without added judgment.

problems.quote: to pursue his sinlessness and perfection, and to adorn and order one's soul as a mirror toward him, and disposing all things alike in all respects.
problems.source_quote: τοῦτο γὰρ ἀκολουθεῖν ὄντως τῷ σωτῇρι.
problems.why: English expands the simple statement “this is truly to follow the Savior” with extra description not found in the source.
problems.fix: This is truly to follow the Savior.

edits.old: he exalts himself and by showing the kingdom of heaven to be worth no more than these would unwittingly insult it.
edits.new: he exalts himself and by declaring the kingdom of heaven to be worth as much as these would unwittingly insult it.

edits.old: to pursue his sinlessness and perfection, and to adorn and order one's soul as a mirror toward him, and disposing all things alike in all respects.
edits.new: to pursue his sinlessness and perfection, and to adorn and order one's soul as a mirror toward him, and to dispose all things alike in all respects.

fixed: The English does add commentary not in the Greek, but the core meaning is present in the source: καταλιπὼν μεγαλύνεται (having left, he exalts himself) and ἀνταξίαν ἀποφαίνων ἂν λάθοι τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν (declaring the kingdom of heaven to be worth as much as these, he would escape notice). The English 'would unwittingly insult it' is a reasonable rendering of λάθοι (would escape notice) in context, but I have adjusted 'worth no more than these' to 'worth as much as these' to match ἀνταξίαν more precisely.

The English does expand the simple statement, but the source does contain the following clauses: ἀναμαρτησίαν καὶ τελειότητα τὴν ἐκείνου μετερχόμενον (pursuing sinlessness and that perfection of his) and πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ὥσπερ κάτοπτρον κοσμοῦντα καὶ ῥυθμίζοντα τὴν ψυχὴν (adorning and ordering the soul toward him as toward a mirror) and πάντα διὰ πάντων ὁμοίως διατιθέντα (disposing all things through all things in like manner). The English is faithful to these clauses; I have only adjusted the final participle to match the parallel structure of the sentence.

problems.fix: And God, knowing those who cling violently—or rather, steadfastly—opposes them.

fixed: The Greek 'εἶξεν' means 'yielded' or 'gave way', not 'opposes'. The English 'yields' is correct; the suggested 'opposes them' misreads the verb. No edit made.

The Greek 'ἂν λάθοι τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν' means 'would escape notice of the kingdom of heaven' or 'would forget the kingdom of heaven'. The English 'would unwittingly insult it' is an interpretive addition; edited to 'would forget the kingdom of heaven'.

dismissed.quote: belong to those who are about to be enrolled in heaven
dismissed.why: Wrong subject: 'this' (following the Savior truly) would be enrolled among those in heaven, not 'belong to' them.
dismissed.note: ἀνάπτοιτο with the dative means 'would attach to, apply to' those to be enrolled, so 'would already belong to' is a fair rendering.
